The addressees are treated as gentiles but their city, assembly structure, and full demographics are not disclosed.
Ephesians and Colossians share extensive language and structure; direction and mechanism of dependence remain debated.
The gender and syntax of “this” in 2:8 do not by themselves identify faith alone as the gift.
Ephesians 2:8-10 joins salvation by grace through faith with creation in Messiah for good works.
The letter depicts the Messiah as peace who makes Jews and gentiles one and creates one new humanity.
Later uses of Ephesians for antisemitism, marital domination, child abuse, slavery, or violent spiritual warfare exceed and can contradict its peace, love, truth, and nonthreatening commands.
Gentile and Jewish believers are portrayed together as citizens, household members, and a growing holy temple.
Ephesians 2:15 describes abolition of the law of commandments in decrees within a reconciliation argument; its scope is disputed.
The former alienation of gentiles must not become antisemitism, supersessionism, or a claim that the church replaces ethnic Israel.
The dividing wall may evoke temple exclusion, Torah boundary, or metaphorical hostility; archaeology does not settle one referent.
Abolition language must not caricature Torah, commandments, Jews, or Judaism as uniquely hostile or legalistic, and it cannot license antisemitism or supersessionism.
One new humanity describes peace without erasing Jewish and gentile histories, ethnicity, embodiment, or present accountability.
Household and temple metaphors describe a community and do not validate nationalism, territorial claims, forced conversion, or sacred-building power.
The foundation of apostles and prophets has multiple readings and cannot alone establish authoritarian succession or clerical immunity.
Dead in trespasses is theological rhetoric, not a diagnosis of disability, depression, trauma, or intellectual incapacity.
Flesh in this argument is not a warrant for body shame, anti-LGBTQ coercion, misogyny, or medical neglect.
Grace through faith and good works resists both earned superiority and claims that ethics, repair, labor justice, or care are irrelevant.
The faith grammar in 2:8 is debated; theology should not be built on the demonstrative pronoun alone.
“Uncircumcision” reports social labeling and cannot license ethnic contempt or coercive circumcision or anti-circumcision.

The operative setting is Roman-period Jerusalem. The inscription is direct evidence for a locally enforced sacred-space boundary and should not be replaced with generic claims about ancient inscriptions or imperial administration.
The warning materializes graded holiness and restricted access within the temple complex while using Greek to address visitors who might not read Hebrew or Aramaic.

The complete stone was found in Jerusalem in 1871 and is held by the Istanbul Archaeology Museums as 2196 T; a fragmentary parallel is held by the Israel Museum. The warning belongs to the Herodian temple horizon before its destruction in 70 CE.
Herodian temple complex in Jerusalem, approximately 23 BCE-70 CE.
Greek-reading visitors approaching restricted areas of the Jerusalem temple complex.
The inscription and Josephus independently describe a boundary separating areas open to foreigners from the more restricted sanctuary precinct.
